why: The behavioural gate recorded one case where HexIDE keeps the doubled quotes VB6 collapses to one, filed as STRING-ESCAPE and read at the time as a continuation-related quirk. It is not: ExpressionExecutor strips the outer quotes with Substring(1, len-2) and does nothing else, so `""` is never unescaped in ANY string literal anywhere. `MsgBox "He said ""hello"""` shows the doubles. That is a wrong value on ordinary code, so the rule needs pinning across the whole shape of the construct rather than at the single point that happened to be measured - especially the degenerate forms, where an off-by-one in the unescape is invisible for a two-character literal and wrong for a one-character one.

cases.why: The ordinary case, and the one real code hits: an escaped quote inside a longer literal. Len as well as the text, because a length is unambiguous where a printed quote is easy to misread.
`""""` - four quote characters denoting one. The minimal escaped literal, and the case an off-by-one unescape gets wrong while still handling longer ones correctly.

`""` is the EMPTY string, not an escaped quote. The pair that distinguishes 'two quotes mean one quote' from 'two quotes mean nothing' depends entirely on whether they are inside a literal or are the whole of it, and an unescape applied to the raw text before stripping the delimiters would get this backwards.
Six quote characters denoting two. Confirms the unescape is a repeated replacement rather than a single one, which a literal containing exactly one escape cannot show.
An escape adjacent to the delimiters on both sides - `"""a"""` is a quote, an a, a quote. The position where confusing a delimiter for an escape is most likely.
`a""b` - an escape with no whitespace either side, so nothing but the quote count decides where the literal ends.

Two literals each carrying an escape, joined. Confirms the unescape happens per literal during evaluation rather than once over the statement text - a whole-line replacement would also 'work' here, so this is paired with the operator case below to tell them apart.
An escaped quote against Chr(34), which is the same character by another route. If these compare equal the unescape is correct in kind and not merely in length.

The original failing case's shape - an escaped quote in a literal on a continued line - kept so the fix is checked against the case that first exposed it, and so a regression there is attributed to escaping rather than to continuations.
